raw_response:
I've been farming these same 30 mu in Quzhou for 50 years, and at 70 I'm not as strong as I used to be, but I know every patch of this land—where the soil is a bit heavier, where it dries out first. My wife and I are the only ones living at home now; our son works in a factory in the county town and can only come back to help for a day or two during the busiest times. That means I have to hire labor for the heavy seasonal work, especially the wheat harvest and maize planting in June—that window is always tight, sometimes just five or six days, and at my age I can't rush like I used to.

For the winter wheat, I'll plant around October 12th. The extension technician always says October 10–15 is the ideal window here, and after five decades I've found that's about right. I'll stick with the improved Jinmai variety I've been using—it's reliable in our conditions, and I saved some seed, but I'll buy fresh certified seed this year to be safe, about 15 kg per mu. For fertilizer, I'll put down a base of compound fertilizer before planting, roughly 25 kg per mu of 15-15-15. That's about 4 kg each of N, P, and K to start with. Then in March at green-up, if the wheat looks yellow from winter, I'll topdress about 8 kg per mu of urea. At jointing stage in April, another 8–10 kg per mu of urea. That brings my nitrogen to around 17 kg per mu total, which is a bit more than the extension recommendation of 15 kg, but I've found that with our soil and the varieties I use, a little extra gives me the yield I need. Phosphorus and potassium come mostly from the base compound fertilizer—maybe 4–5 kg per mu each. I split the nitrogen three ways because putting it all down at once is wasteful; some always leaches before the roots can take it up.

For wheat irrigation, I have a tube well, but the electricity for pumping keeps getting more expensive. Still, wheat needs water at the right times. I'll irrigate once before winter if the soil is dry after planting, once at green-up in spring, once at jointing, and if May is dry, once more at grain filling. That's usually 3–4 times. I can't afford to skip it—drought at jointing will cost me more than the pumping bill.

For summer maize, the key is speed after wheat harvest in mid-June. I'll hire a combine for the wheat, and then I need to get the maize in the ground within a few days. I use a no-till planter or minimal tillage into the wheat stubble—there's no time for deep plowing, and honestly at my age I prefer not to do heavy tillage anyway. I'll plant a hybrid variety, probably Zhengdan 958 or something similar the seed dealer recommends, about 2.5 kg per mu. For fertilizer, I band compound fertilizer at planting, about 20 kg per mu, and then at the big trumpet stage—when the plants have 10–12 leaves—I topdress with urea, about 12–15 kg per mu. That gives me roughly 15 kg N per mu total for the maize, plus some P and K from the base. Maize doesn't need as much irrigation as wheat; I'll water at planting if it's dry, and once at big trumpet. If the summer rains are good, that might be enough.

For pesticides, I use herbicide on both crops—once in early spring for wheat, and once for maize shortly after emergence. For maize, I keep an eye out for corn borer; if I see signs, I'll spray insecticide, but I don't do it preventively every year. The cost adds up.

Labor is my biggest constraint after land. My wife and I can handle fertilizing, irrigating, spraying, and monitoring—maybe 20 days of our own labor for wheat and 18 for maize. But for harvesting wheat, planting maize in that tight window, and harvesting maize in October, I need hired hands. I'll need about 8 hired days for wheat harvest and early work, and 12 hired days for the maize planting rush and harvest. At roughly 120–150 yuan per day, that's a significant cost, but there's no other way with just the two of us.

Total input costs—seed, fertilizer, pesticide, hired labor, pumping electricity—will run me about 17,000 yuan for the year. That's a lot of cash to put out upfront, especially since I'm on a fixed budget. I could maybe push the fertilizer a bit higher for better yield, but at my age I prefer stability. I'd rather apply a safe amount and get a reliable crop than gamble on maximizing yield and risk a big loss if the weather turns. I'm targeting about 450 kg per mu for wheat and 500 kg per mu for maize. If prices hold and we don't get a bad drought, that should see us through the year.
